newsitem.title: USA: Treasury official sees bank antitrust renaissance.
newsitem.headline: Treasury official sees bank antitrust renaissance.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury Department official said on Thursday that near-dormant antitrust rules for banks could begin to limit industry consolidation as giant institutions come to dominate local banking markets.
Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke told a business dinner at the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta that consolidation has eliminated local competition by many independent institutions.

"As we see these major regional and nationwide organizations now meeting one another in local markets around the country, it holds out to me the prospect that antitrust is going to begin to come back to life," Hawke said.
"It will end up being a constraint on the degree of consolidation among large companies," he added.

U.S. antitrust rules, which actively regulated local market competition in the 1960s, lapsed into near-dormancy a decade ago as banking companies extended their operations into new markets and finally crossed state boundaries.

"Now, what's happening is that the wheel is coming around full circle, and many of the local markets throughout the country have lost a lot of their smaller, independent banks," Hawke told his audience.
"There might well be a renaissance of antitrust," he said.
